name: Tectospinal tract
modality: reflex turning of the head toward stimuli
summary: Neurons of the deep layers of the superior colliculus send axons that cross in the dorsal tegmental decussation just below the periaqueductal gray, descend near the MLF through the brainstem and end in the cervical cord, where they drive neck motor neurons to turn the head toward a visual, auditory or somatosensory stimulus. It is the spinal component of the orienting response and works with the tectobulbar fibers that move the eyes toward the same target, so that gaze and head turn arrive together and the fovea lands on whatever attracted attention.

origin.note: Deep and intermediate layers of the superior colliculus, driven by retinal, auditory and cortical input.

decussation.note: Crosses beneath the periaqueductal gray at the level of the colliculi.

termination: Motor neurons and interneurons of the upper cervical cord for neck muscles.

lesionEffectsByLevel.effects: Impaired reflex orienting of the head and eyes to the contralateral side; rarely isolated
Orienting deficits merge with the vertical gaze palsy of the Parinaud syndrome

pearls: This tract is why a sudden sound makes you turn your head before you know why
Isolated tectospinal lesions are a textbook concept rather than a clinical entity; think of it as part of the dorsal midbrain
